note: Sherwood Anderson acted as an early mentor, encouraged Hemingway's fiction, and helped connect him to literary contacts as Hemingway entered the Paris literary world.

note: Stein was a formative Paris contact; scholarship credits Hemingway with absorbing aspects of her repetitive, colloquial-seeming prose while their relationship also involved mutual exchange and later conflict.
Pound helped shape Hemingway's early craft through Imagist attention to the accurate image and aggressive removal of unnecessary modifiers; their educational relationship was not purely one-way.
Hemingway said he learned about writing from painters as well as writers, and Cézanne was a particular favorite; critics have connected this visual discipline to his prose method.

Hemingway's first newspaper job exposed him to the Kansas City Star's crisp reporting conventions: short sentences, vigorous English, immediacy, and restraint with adjectives. The edge records a professional style environment rather than claiming the style sheet alone created his mature prose.

After World War I Hemingway lived and worked in Paris among the expatriate writers and artists later grouped as the Lost Generation; this network provided a dense environment of reading, criticism, publishing, and artistic exchange.
source_label: Library of Congress — Hemingway in Paris

note: Hemingway served as a Red Cross ambulance driver in Italy during World War I and was badly wounded. The relationship records direct lived experience that repeatedly entered his fiction and ideas about war.
source_label: Library of Congress — Today in History: Ernest Hemingway

note: Poe's early poetry and recurring interests in melancholy, visionary imagination, beauty, and subjective extremity developed within the Romantic literary field.
Poetry Foundation identifies Radcliffe's Gothic novels among the earlier literary influences visible in Poe's use of the grotesque, demonic, terror, and Gothic atmosphere.
Hoffmann's uncanny and grotesque fantastic tales form part of Poe's documented literary ancestry, although scholarship debates the exact degree and route of direct borrowing.
Poe's early verse reflects a strong Byronic model, including the melancholy, alienated hero and the tone of poems such as Childe Harold's Pilgrimage.
Poe's early poetry reflects the influence of Keats alongside Byron and Shelley, especially within the Romantic preoccupation with beauty, mortality, and poetic imagination.
Poe admired Shelley and his early poetry drew on Shelleyan Romantic models; this is a documented literary influence rather than a claim of one-to-one borrowing.
Blackwood's concentrated tales of terror provided Poe and other nineteenth-century writers with a recognizable short-form model that Poe emulated, parodied, and transformed.
source_label: Cambridge University Press — Blackwood's and Poe

note: Poe inherited and transformed an established British and transatlantic Gothic tradition rather than inventing Gothic horror ex nihilo.

note: Edgar Allan Poe wrote The Fall of the House of Usher.
